messages.subject: Writing custom samplers
parts:
Hey everyone, 

I am trying to write a custom MCMC sampler in NIMBLE to produce objective priors for N-mixture models, but I am having some errors and trouble understanding NIMBLE's syntax.  My code is  as follows:

library(nimble)

#approximation function
approximation = nimbleFunction(
  run = function(theta0 = double(0), theta= double(0), prev = double(0), c = double(0)){
    returnType(double(0))
    ap = prev + (theta-theta0)*sqrt(c*exp(prev)-2*(1+prev)) + (theta-theta0)^2*(c*exp(prev)-2)/4 + (theta-theta0)^3/6*c*exp(prev)*sqrt(c*exp(prev)-2*(1+prev))/2
    return(ap)
  }
)

#N-mixture likelihood function

myncol = nimbleRcall(function(x=double(2)){}, Rfun = 'ncol', returnType = double(0) )
mynrow = nimbleRcall(function(x=double(2)){}, Rfun = 'nrow', returnType = double(0) )
mycolSums = nimbleRcall(function(x = double(2)){}, Rfun = 'colSums', returnType = double(0) )

Nmixlik = nimbleFunction(
  run= function(y = double(2), p = double(0), lambda = double(0), N = double(1)){
    returnType(double(0))
    T <- myncol(y)
    R <- mynrow(y)
    bin1.aux <- nimMatrix(0, ncol = T, nrow = R)
    f1 <- nimNumeric(R)
    b <- nimMatrix(0, ncol = T, nrow = R )
    
    for (i in 1:R) {
      f1[i] <- dpois(N[i], lambda)
      for (j in 1:T) bin1.aux[i, j] <- dbinom(y[i, j], N[i], p, log = TRUE)
    }
    
    for (i in 1:T) {
      b[,i] <-  bin1.aux[,i]+ f1
    }
    
    return(sum(mycolSums(b)))
    
  }
)


# M-H for parameter space of p, ie (0,1)
#c =2 and u(0) =1.31
# p is the target

p_OBp_sampler <- nimbleFunction(
  
  contains = sampler_BASE,
  
  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control){
    scale <- 0.1
    N <- model[["N"]]
    lambda <- model[["lambda"]]
    y <- model$C
    prevp <- model[["mup"]]
    c <- 2
  },
  
  run = function(){
    
    # draw theta from proposal distribtuion
    proposal <- rnorm(1, model[[target]], scale)
    
    #approximate 
    num_app <- approximation(model[[target]], proposal,prevp,c)
    
    # compute prior fraction
    frac_p <- -(num_app-prevp)
    
    #log Metropolis Hasting ratio
    log_MH_ratio <- Nmixlik(y,proposal,lambda,N) - Nmixlik(y,model[[target]],lambda,N) + frac_p 
    
    # M-H step- determine whether or not to accept the newly proposed value. Can also use the decide function
    u <- runif(1,0,1)
    if(u < exp(log_MH_ratio)) jump <- TRUE
    else                      jump <- FALSE
    
      # store proposal into the model
      model[[target]] <<- proposal
      
      # store value of mup in model 
      model[["mup"]] <<- num_app
   
    # keep the model and mvSaved objects consistent    
    if(jump) copy(from = model, to = mvSaved,nodes = c("p", "mup"), row = 1, logProb = FALSE) 
    else copy(from = mvSaved, to = model,nodes = c("p", "mup"), row = 1, logProb = FALSE)
    
  },
  
  methods = list(reset = function(){})
)

The objective prior that I am trying to implement is not model-based, it depends on the parameter space and has to be computed numerically. The MCMC is a Metropolis-Hasting.  My question is then in writing the sampler, how do I store the values accepted from the Metropolis-Hasting? I am not sure what the arguments of the copy function do. Depending on whether the proposal is accepted or not, I also want to store num_app as this is used in the next iteration of the sampler. How can I do this? I've looked at the example provided in the manual and some examples in this group but there are not many details. Many thanks for explaining. 


I've used the above code to change the sampler of p to my custom sampler  for the N-mixture model:

  # Priors

parts:
Hi Fabian,

There are a bunch of things going on here.

I think the immediate source of the error is that you declared the nimbleRcall for mycolSums to be scalar, but it should be a vector.  However, it looks like you shouldn't need it anyway.

Use of nimbleRcall will always impose a performance penalty.  You can get what you want by dim(y)[1], dim(y)[2] and sum(b), which will sum over both dimensions.  Also, I think your Nmixlik function will be more efficient if you don't form b and bin1.aux at all.  I think you could accumulate the sums as you go.

You can always test nimbleFunctions, either uncompiled or compiled, outside of their use in a model.

In p_OBp_sampler, you are assuming N, lambda, C and mup in the model will never change.  That's because you extract those values in the setup code, but setup code is only evaluated once, when the nimbleFunction is specialized.  In this case that will happen during buildMCMC.  If those values might differ every time you call the sampler, I'm guessing you want to extract them in the run code.

I not clearly following how you want the value calculated from Nmixlik to relate to the model.  If you want a custom distribution, you can modify Nmixlik and use it directly in the model (perhaps N[i] ~ Nmixlik(...)?).  Every stochastic node in the model has an associated logProb value.  Usually the nimCopy after an accept/reject decision uses logProb = TRUE to cache those logProb values.  If you have other values you need to cache, you can either make a variable in setup code and use that, because that will be like a class member data, or you can make a variable in the model and use that as a cache location.

The best source of ideas for how samplers work is the source code for nimble's built-in samplers.  Here is our basic Metropolis-Hasting sampler: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R#L146 Unfortunately there is a fair bit of code to accomplish the adaptation (self-tuning of the proposal standard deviation), but the core propose-accept-reject steps are in the run code.

A good way to see what is happening and learn more about nimble is to run the MCMC in R (uncompiled) and use standard R debugging tools.  For example, you can put a browser() in the run code of your sampler and then step through it each time it is called.

I haven't followed exactly where you are stuck, but it's great to see this application.  I hope this helped and let us know more questions.

We haven't advertised widely because we're going to udpate it soon, but we have put some relevant ecology distributions in a package here: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimbleEcology  It includes a dNmixture distribution that might be useful for you.  However, we have a paper coming out showing that in some cases marginalization makes MCMC more efficient and in other cases not.  The dNmixture marginalization can be fairly costly, so it may not be more efficient.

HTH
-Perry

Hi Fabian,

There are a bunch of things going on here.

I think the immediate source of the error is that you declared the nimbleRcall for mycolSums to be scalar, but it should be a vector.  However, it looks like you shouldn't need it anyway.

Use of nimbleRcall will always impose a performance penalty.  You can get what you want by dim(y)[1], dim(y)[2] and sum(b), which will sum over both dimensions.  Also, I think your Nmixlik function will be more efficient if you don't form b and bin1.aux at all.  I think you could accumulate the sums as you go.

You can always test nimbleFunctions, either uncompiled or compiled, outside of their use in a model.

In p_OBp_sampler, you are assuming N, lambda, C and mup in the model will never change.  That's because you extract those values in the setup code, but setup code is only evaluated once, when the nimbleFunction is specialized.  In this case that will happen during buildMCMC.  If those values might differ every time you call the sampler, I'm guessing you want to extract them in the run code.

I not clearly following how you want the value calculated from Nmixlik to relate to the model.  If you want a custom distribution, you can modify Nmixlik and use it directly in the model (perhaps N[i] ~ Nmixlik(...)?).  Every stochastic node in the model has an associated logProb value.  Usually the nimCopy after an accept/reject decision uses logProb = TRUE to cache those logProb values.  If you have other values you need to cache, you can either make a variable in setup code and use that, because that will be like a class member data, or you can make a variable in the model and use that as a cache location.

The best source of ideas for how samplers work is the source code for nimble's built-in samplers.  Here is our basic Metropolis-Hasting sampler: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R#L146 Unfortunately there is a fair bit of code to accomplish the adaptation (self-tuning of the proposal standard deviation), but the core propose-accept-reject steps are in the run code.

A good way to see what is happening and learn more about nimble is to run the MCMC in R (uncompiled) and use standard R debugging tools.  For example, you can put a browser() in the run code of your sampler and then step through it each time it is called.

I haven't followed exactly where you are stuck, but it's great to see this application.  I hope this helped and let us know more questions.

We haven't advertised widely because we're going to udpate it soon, but we have put some relevant ecology distributions in a package here: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimbleEcology  It includes a dNmixture distribution that might be useful for you.  However, we have a paper coming out showing that in some cases marginalization makes MCMC more efficient and in other cases not.  The dNmixture marginalization can be fairly costly, so it may not be more efficient.

HTH
-Perry

Hi Fabian,

We had some off-list discussion of this, and now I want to reply on list for anyone else interested in this thread.

model$getLogProb(myNodes) will return the sum of cached logProb values for any stochastic nodes in myNodes.  The default for myNodes is the entire model.

To explain a little more, relevant also to the nimCopy question, each stochastic node has an associated log probability density (logProb) value.  The model is like a machine you control.  model$calculate(myNodes) will calculate myNodes in order.  For stochastic nodes, that means it will calculate and store the logProb value.  We refer to the stored logProb values as being cached.  It will also return the sum of the logProb values of the stochastic nodes in myNodes.  model$getLogProb(myNodes) returns the sum of logProbs for the same nodes, but it does not actually calculate them.  It just uses the cached values, which typically were stored by the most recent call to model$calculate(myNodes).  For MCMC sampler purposes, usually the logProbs for the "current" state can be accessed by model$getLogProb, while those for the "proposed" state need to be calculated by model$calculate; see more below.

I haven't had time to go over the paper you linked to.  Typically, a good design for a new prior is to write it as a nimbleFunction provided as a user-defined distribution (User Manual, Ch. 12).  You can have that return any value that you want to be used as a "logProb", even if it is not actually a log probability density.  However, if it is not so simple, then what you are doing could be a good design.  It looks like the 'approximation' function needs both the proposed and current values, in which case a user-defined distribution would not be adequate, and building the prior logic into the sampler is a fine solution.

It looks like you are doing log probability calculations outside of the model, which is not ideal.  I am not 100% sure but I think a possibly better design would be the following:

Make N-mixture likelihood a user-defined distribution for the counts (similar to the code for Ponisio et al. that I sent on this list recently, and similar to what our updated nimbleEcology package will have).  You would have something like
counts[i, 1:T] ~ dNmixture(<various parameters>)
if counts[i, 1:T] are say the counts from T sampling occasions at site i.

I assume that p is what you want to custom sample and that it will be a parameter of your dNmixture distribution.

Then in the custom sampler, setup code would have "calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)" and run code would use "model$getLogProb(calcNodes)" to access the sum of logProbs currently in the model (without the cost of calculating them).  After you put the proposal value of p in the model, "model$calculate(calcNodes)" would return the sum of logProbs with the proposal value of p.

mvSaved is a modelValues object with values for all model nodes and logProbs (which exist only for stochastic nodes).  modelValues is a class for storing multiple sets of values of multiple model variables. For example, mcmc samples are stored in a modelValues object.  Each set of values is called a "row" because we often think of MCMC samples with rows for iterations and columns for nodes. In the case of mvSaved, it needs only one row.  A sampler can assume upon entry that mvSaved and the model are in sync, meaning they have all the same values.  Upon exit, a sampler must leave mvSaved and the model in sync again, possibly with new values as a result of the sampler's update.  When we say mvSaved, we mean the one and only row of mvSaved, since it only needs and only has one row.  During a typical sampler's run steps, it will put some proposal value(s) in the model and call model$calculate.  At this point, mvSaved will be out of sync with model.  If the proposal is to be accepted, typically one copies from the model (which still has the proposal and results of model$calculate) to mvSaved.  If the proposal is to be rejected, typically one copies from mvSaved to the model.

Your first use of nimCopy should include calcNodes because other nodes will not have been modified.  Only nodes modified by model$calculate need to be copied.  In your case, I'm not sure any nodes are modified by llFunction$run(), but if you make use of the model instead of going around it (which is ok, but nonstandard), then you'll have something that needs copying.  But also I don't think you need the log_MH_ratio == -Inf clause at all, because if that is true then the result of decide() later should be 0 (FALSE).  In built-in samplers that you might be looking at, we typically have a step of checking for a -Inf, but typically this is only for the logProb(s) of the target node(s), i.e. their priors.  We check that before calculating dependencies because if a proposal steps outside of valid values for the target, for example, we can reject without calculating everything else.  The later nimCopys look fine, except that they aren't necessary because I think you aren't (yet) using the model in any way except for modifying the target node.  If you are able to re-arrange as suggest above, then you'll have more meaningful copying to do.  What I can't tell from the code is whether this non-standard scheme will mess up other samplers, for example samplers on values of N that might depend on calculations based on p, which would not have been updated in mvSamples upon exit of your sampler, thereby violating the rules for new sampers. 

A good strategy for understanding the system is to run *uncompiled*.  Everything will work uncompiled, in which case execution is in pure R.  That means for example that you can put a browser() in the run code of your custom sampler and study the state of the model or whatever else is of interest.  You can access values of the model and modelValues in typical R syntax, covered in the User Manual.  You can also call nimCopy or do other steps directly from the command line if you need to study how they work by experiment.  

I'm not sure of how "mup" fits in the graph (model), but ideally what one wants is to have everything logically in the model and then let algorithms use model-generic programming (for example determining relevant nodes by model$getDependencies) to use every model correctly.  So we try to avoid work-arounds like c(calcNodes, "mup"), but they are perfectly fine if you know what you are doing and this one case is all you want to work.

I hope that all helps.

-Perry

On Thu, Feb 13, 2020 at 11:34 PM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
Hi Fabian,

There are a bunch of things going on here.

I think the immediate source of the error is that you declared the nimbleRcall for mycolSums to be scalar, but it should be a vector.  However, it looks like you shouldn't need it anyway.

Use of nimbleRcall will always impose a performance penalty.  You can get what you want by dim(y)[1], dim(y)[2] and sum(b), which will sum over both dimensions.  Also, I think your Nmixlik function will be more efficient if you don't form b and bin1.aux at all.  I think you could accumulate the sums as you go.

You can always test nimbleFunctions, either uncompiled or compiled, outside of their use in a model.

In p_OBp_sampler, you are assuming N, lambda, C and mup in the model will never change.  That's because you extract those values in the setup code, but setup code is only evaluated once, when the nimbleFunction is specialized.  In this case that will happen during buildMCMC.  If those values might differ every time you call the sampler, I'm guessing you want to extract them in the run code.

I not clearly following how you want the value calculated from Nmixlik to relate to the model.  If you want a custom distribution, you can modify Nmixlik and use it directly in the model (perhaps N[i] ~ Nmixlik(...)?).  Every stochastic node in the model has an associated logProb value.  Usually the nimCopy after an accept/reject decision uses logProb = TRUE to cache those logProb values.  If you have other values you need to cache, you can either make a variable in setup code and use that, because that will be like a class member data, or you can make a variable in the model and use that as a cache location.

The best source of ideas for how samplers work is the source code for nimble's built-in samplers.  Here is our basic Metropolis-Hasting sampler: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R#L146 Unfortunately there is a fair bit of code to accomplish the adaptation (self-tuning of the proposal standard deviation), but the core propose-accept-reject steps are in the run code.

A good way to see what is happening and learn more about nimble is to run the MCMC in R (uncompiled) and use standard R debugging tools.  For example, you can put a browser() in the run code of your sampler and then step through it each time it is called.

I haven't followed exactly where you are stuck, but it's great to see this application.  I hope this helped and let us know more questions.

We haven't advertised widely because we're going to udpate it soon, but we have put some relevant ecology distributions in a package here: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimbleEcology  It includes a dNmixture distribution that might be useful for you.  However, we have a paper coming out showing that in some cases marginalization makes MCMC more efficient and in other cases not.  The dNmixture marginalization can be fairly costly, so it may not be more efficient.

HTH
-Perry

Hi Fabian,

We had some off-list discussion of this, and now I want to reply on list for anyone else interested in this thread.

model$getLogProb(myNodes) will return the sum of cached logProb values for any stochastic nodes in myNodes.  The default for myNodes is the entire model.

To explain a little more, relevant also to the nimCopy question, each stochastic node has an associated log probability density (logProb) value.  The model is like a machine you control.  model$calculate(myNodes) will calculate myNodes in order.  For stochastic nodes, that means it will calculate and store the logProb value.  We refer to the stored logProb values as being cached.  It will also return the sum of the logProb values of the stochastic nodes in myNodes.  model$getLogProb(myNodes) returns the sum of logProbs for the same nodes, but it does not actually calculate them.  It just uses the cached values, which typically were stored by the most recent call to model$calculate(myNodes).  For MCMC sampler purposes, usually the logProbs for the "current" state can be accessed by model$getLogProb, while those for the "proposed" state need to be calculated by model$calculate; see more below.

I haven't had time to go over the paper you linked to.  Typically, a good design for a new prior is to write it as a nimbleFunction provided as a user-defined distribution (User Manual, Ch. 12).  You can have that return any value that you want to be used as a "logProb", even if it is not actually a log probability density.  However, if it is not so simple, then what you are doing could be a good design.  It looks like the 'approximation' function needs both the proposed and current values, in which case a user-defined distribution would not be adequate, and building the prior logic into the sampler is a fine solution.

It looks like you are doing log probability calculations outside of the model, which is not ideal.  I am not 100% sure but I think a possibly better design would be the following:

Make N-mixture likelihood a user-defined distribution for the counts (similar to the code for Ponisio et al. that I sent on this list recently, and similar to what our updated nimbleEcology package will have).  You would have something like
counts[i, 1:T] ~ dNmixture(<various parameters>)
if counts[i, 1:T] are say the counts from T sampling occasions at site i.

I assume that p is what you want to custom sample and that it will be a parameter of your dNmixture distribution.

Then in the custom sampler, setup code would have "calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)" and run code would use "model$getLogProb(calcNodes)" to access the sum of logProbs currently in the model (without the cost of calculating them).  After you put the proposal value of p in the model, "model$calculate(calcNodes)" would return the sum of logProbs with the proposal value of p.

mvSaved is a modelValues object with values for all model nodes and logProbs (which exist only for stochastic nodes).  modelValues is a class for storing multiple sets of values of multiple model variables. For example, mcmc samples are stored in a modelValues object.  Each set of values is called a "row" because we often think of MCMC samples with rows for iterations and columns for nodes. In the case of mvSaved, it needs only one row.  A sampler can assume upon entry that mvSaved and the model are in sync, meaning they have all the same values.  Upon exit, a sampler must leave mvSaved and the model in sync again, possibly with new values as a result of the sampler's update.  When we say mvSaved, we mean the one and only row of mvSaved, since it only needs and only has one row.  During a typical sampler's run steps, it will put some proposal value(s) in the model and call model$calculate.  At this point, mvSaved will be out of sync with model.  If the proposal is to be accepted, typically one copies from the model (which still has the proposal and results of model$calculate) to mvSaved.  If the proposal is to be rejected, typically one copies from mvSaved to the model.

Your first use of nimCopy should include calcNodes because other nodes will not have been modified.  Only nodes modified by model$calculate need to be copied.  In your case, I'm not sure any nodes are modified by llFunction$run(), but if you make use of the model instead of going around it (which is ok, but nonstandard), then you'll have something that needs copying.  But also I don't think you need the log_MH_ratio == -Inf clause at all, because if that is true then the result of decide() later should be 0 (FALSE).  In built-in samplers that you might be looking at, we typically have a step of checking for a -Inf, but typically this is only for the logProb(s) of the target node(s), i.e. their priors.  We check that before calculating dependencies because if a proposal steps outside of valid values for the target, for example, we can reject without calculating everything else.  The later nimCopys look fine, except that they aren't necessary because I think you aren't (yet) using the model in any way except for modifying the target node.  If you are able to re-arrange as suggest above, then you'll have more meaningful copying to do.  What I can't tell from the code is whether this non-standard scheme will mess up other samplers, for example samplers on values of N that might depend on calculations based on p, which would not have been updated in mvSamples upon exit of your sampler, thereby violating the rules for new sampers. 

A good strategy for understanding the system is to run *uncompiled*.  Everything will work uncompiled, in which case execution is in pure R.  That means for example that you can put a browser() in the run code of your custom sampler and study the state of the model or whatever else is of interest.  You can access values of the model and modelValues in typical R syntax, covered in the User Manual.  You can also call nimCopy or do other steps directly from the command line if you need to study how they work by experiment.  

I'm not sure of how "mup" fits in the graph (model), but ideally what one wants is to have everything logically in the model and then let algorithms use model-generic programming (for example determining relevant nodes by model$getDependencies) to use every model correctly.  So we try to avoid work-arounds like c(calcNodes, "mup"), but they are perfectly fine if you know what you are doing and this one case is all you want to work.

I hope that all helps.

-Perry

There are a bunch of things going on here.

I think the immediate source of the error is that you declared the nimbleRcall for mycolSums to be scalar, but it should be a vector.  However, it looks like you shouldn't need it anyway.

Use of nimbleRcall will always impose a performance penalty.  You can get what you want by dim(y)[1], dim(y)[2] and sum(b), which will sum over both dimensions.  Also, I think your Nmixlik function will be more efficient if you don't form b and bin1.aux at all.  I think you could accumulate the sums as you go.

You can always test nimbleFunctions, either uncompiled or compiled, outside of their use in a model.

In p_OBp_sampler, you are assuming N, lambda, C and mup in the model will never change.  That's because you extract those values in the setup code, but setup code is only evaluated once, when the nimbleFunction is specialized.  In this case that will happen during buildMCMC.  If those values might differ every time you call the sampler, I'm guessing you want to extract them in the run code.

I not clearly following how you want the value calculated from Nmixlik to relate to the model.  If you want a custom distribution, you can modify Nmixlik and use it directly in the model (perhaps N[i] ~ Nmixlik(...)?).  Every stochastic node in the model has an associated logProb value.  Usually the nimCopy after an accept/reject decision uses logProb = TRUE to cache those logProb values.  If you have other values you need to cache, you can either make a variable in setup code and use that, because that will be like a class member data, or you can make a variable in the model and use that as a cache location.

Hi Fabian,

We had some off-list discussion of this, and now I want to reply on list for anyone else interested in this thread.

model$getLogProb(myNodes) will return the sum of cached logProb values for any stochastic nodes in myNodes.  The default for myNodes is the entire model.

To explain a little more, relevant also to the nimCopy question, each stochastic node has an associated log probability density (logProb) value.  The model is like a machine you control.  model$calculate(myNodes) will calculate myNodes in order.  For stochastic nodes, that means it will calculate and store the logProb value.  We refer to the stored logProb values as being cached.  It will also return the sum of the logProb values of the stochastic nodes in myNodes.  model$getLogProb(myNodes) returns the sum of logProbs for the same nodes, but it does not actually calculate them.  It just uses the cached values, which typically were stored by the most recent call to model$calculate(myNodes).  For MCMC sampler purposes, usually the logProbs for the "current" state can be accessed by model$getLogProb, while those for the "proposed" state need to be calculated by model$calculate; see more below.

I haven't had time to go over the paper you linked to.  Typically, a good design for a new prior is to write it as a nimbleFunction provided as a user-defined distribution (User Manual, Ch. 12).  You can have that return any value that you want to be used as a "logProb", even if it is not actually a log probability density.  However, if it is not so simple, then what you are doing could be a good design.  It looks like the 'approximation' function needs both the proposed and current values, in which case a user-defined distribution would not be adequate, and building the prior logic into the sampler is a fine solution.

It looks like you are doing log probability calculations outside of the model, which is not ideal.  I am not 100% sure but I think a possibly better design would be the following:

Make N-mixture likelihood a user-defined distribution for the counts (similar to the code for Ponisio et al. that I sent on this list recently, and similar to what our updated nimbleEcology package will have).  You would have something like
counts[i, 1:T] ~ dNmixture(<various parameters>)
if counts[i, 1:T] are say the counts from T sampling occasions at site i.

I assume that p is what you want to custom sample and that it will be a parameter of your dNmixture distribution.

Then in the custom sampler, setup code would have "calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)" and run code would use "model$getLogProb(calcNodes)" to access the sum of logProbs currently in the model (without the cost of calculating them).  After you put the proposal value of p in the model, "model$calculate(calcNodes)" would return the sum of logProbs with the proposal value of p.

mvSaved is a modelValues object with values for all model nodes and logProbs (which exist only for stochastic nodes).  modelValues is a class for storing multiple sets of values of multiple model variables. For example, mcmc samples are stored in a modelValues object.  Each set of values is called a "row" because we often think of MCMC samples with rows for iterations and columns for nodes. In the case of mvSaved, it needs only one row.  A sampler can assume upon entry that mvSaved and the model are in sync, meaning they have all the same values.  Upon exit, a sampler must leave mvSaved and the model in sync again, possibly with new values as a result of the sampler's update.  When we say mvSaved, we mean the one and only row of mvSaved, since it only needs and only has one row.  During a typical sampler's run steps, it will put some proposal value(s) in the model and call model$calculate.  At this point, mvSaved will be out of sync with model.  If the proposal is to be accepted, typically one copies from the model (which still has the proposal and results of model$calculate) to mvSaved.  If the proposal is to be rejected, typically one copies from mvSaved to the model.

Your first use of nimCopy should include calcNodes because other nodes will not have been modified.  Only nodes modified by model$calculate need to be copied.  In your case, I'm not sure any nodes are modified by llFunction$run(), but if you make use of the model instead of going around it (which is ok, but nonstandard), then you'll have something that needs copying.  But also I don't think you need the log_MH_ratio == -Inf clause at all, because if that is true then the result of decide() later should be 0 (FALSE).  In built-in samplers that you might be looking at, we typically have a step of checking for a -Inf, but typically this is only for the logProb(s) of the target node(s), i.e. their priors.  We check that before calculating dependencies because if a proposal steps outside of valid values for the target, for example, we can reject without calculating everything else.  The later nimCopys look fine, except that they aren't necessary because I think you aren't (yet) using the model in any way except for modifying the target node.  If you are able to re-arrange as suggest above, then you'll have more meaningful copying to do.  What I can't tell from the code is whether this non-standard scheme will mess up other samplers, for example samplers on values of N that might depend on calculations based on p, which would not have been updated in mvSamples upon exit of your sampler, thereby violating the rules for new sampers. 

A good strategy for understanding the system is to run *uncompiled*.  Everything will work uncompiled, in which case execution is in pure R.  That means for example that you can put a browser() in the run code of your custom sampler and study the state of the model or whatever else is of interest.  You can access values of the model and modelValues in typical R syntax, covered in the User Manual.  You can also call nimCopy or do other steps directly from the command line if you need to study how they work by experiment.  

I'm not sure of how "mup" fits in the graph (model), but ideally what one wants is to have everything logically in the model and then let algorithms use model-generic programming (for example determining relevant nodes by model$getDependencies) to use every model correctly.  So we try to avoid work-arounds like c(calcNodes, "mup"), but they are perfectly fine if you know what you are doing and this one case is all you want to work.

I hope that all helps.

-Perry
